title: Protocol for the production and reconstitution of VDAC1 for functional assays
author: Dearden, Ravishankar, et al.
materials: Amicon Ultra 15 mL centrifugal filter, 10K MWCO

steps.title: Isolate and denature inclusion bodies
steps.instruction: Harvest inclusion bodies from thawed cells, wash, solubilize in 8 M urea, and clarify the lysate for downstream Ni‑NTA purification.

substeps.instruction: Thaw frozen cell pellet at 20 °C–24 °C (cells were stored at –20 °C).
Add lysozyme (3–30 mg total) to reach 0.1–1.0 mg mL⁻¹; incubate 10 min at 20 °C–24 °C on a rotating/rocking shaker.
Add Triton X‑100 to 0.6 % (v/v) (add 1.5 mL of 10 % (v/v) stock); incubate 10 min at 20 °C–24 °C on a rotating/rocking shaker.

Sonicate on ice with a probe sonicator: 3 min at 50 % amplitude, 50 % duty cycle; rest 1 min on ice; repeat three times (total 9 min sonication, 4.5 min “on”). Avoid overheating, foaming, glass vessels, and wear ear protection.
Centrifuge lysate at 12 000 × g for 15 min at 20 °C–24 °C.
Save 3 µL of supernatant for SDS‑PAGE (label “Supernatant”). Discard the remainder of the supernatant.
Resuspend the white pellet in 30 mL Inclusion Bodies Wash Buffer; vortex briefly.
Transfer to a 40 mL glass homogenizer and break clumps with ≥10 strokes of a loose‑fitting pestle (more strokes if needed).
Re‑pellet by centrifugation at 12 000 × g for 15 min at 20 °C–24 °C.
Discard supernatant and resuspend pellet in 30 mL Equilibration Buffer (contains 8 M urea); vortex and give ≥10 homogenizer strokes.
Transfer back to a centrifuge tube and solubilize inclusion bodies in Equilibration Buffer for ≥1 h at 20 °C–24 °C on a rotating/rocking shaker (pause point: can extend to 16–20 h).
Centrifuge solubilized material at 25 000 × g for 45 min at 20 °C–24 °C (Ni‑NTA resin can be prepared during this spin).
Save 3 µL of the clarified supernatant for SDS‑PAGE (label “Load”) and keep the remainder for Ni‑NTA affinity chromatography.
Estimated duration: 0.5 day.

steps.title: Nickel affinity purification of denatured VDAC1
steps.instruction: Bind solubilized His‑tagged VDAC1 to Ni‑NTA resin, wash, and elute with imidazole while monitoring A₂₈₀.

substeps.instruction: Transfer 10 mL bed volume of Ni‑NTA resin to a ≥40 mL gravity‑flow column (glass or plastic).
Wash resin with 5 column volumes (CV; 50 mL) de‑ionized water, then with 5 CV Equilibration Buffer.
Add 120 µL of 5 M imidazole to the solubilized inclusion bodies (from step 13) to reach a final imidazole concentration of 20 mM.
Cap the bottom of the column, load the imidazole‑adjusted lysate onto the equilibrated resin, cap the top, and verify watertightness (wrap ends with Parafilm if needed).
Incubate the column for 1 h at 20 °C–24 °C on a rotating/rocking shaker.
Collect the flow‑through in a 50 mL conical tube; save 3 µL for SDS‑PAGE (label “Flow Through”).
Wash the column with Ni‑NTA Wash Buffer (20 mM imidazole) until A₂₈₀ reaches baseline (≈0; usually within ~5 CV). Collect wash in a 50 mL tube and save 3 µL for SDS‑PAGE (label “Wash”).
Elute VDAC1 with 3–5 CV Ni‑NTA Elution Buffer (150 mM imidazole); collect 5 mL fractions.
Measure A₂₈₀ of each fraction in a quartz cuvette; continue washing until A₂₈₀ returns to baseline (≈3–5 CV, 6–10 fractions). Most protein elutes within 2 CV.
Calculate protein concentration using Beer‑Lambert law: ε₂₈₀ = 32 500 M⁻¹ cm⁻¹, pathlength = 1 cm (e.g., A₂₈₀ = 1.0 → 31 µM). Use quartz cuvettes only and rinse thoroughly between samples.
Estimated duration: 0.5 day.

steps.title: Run SDS-PAGE analysis of samples
steps.instruction: Assess purity of each purification fraction by SDS‑PAGE and Coomassie staining.

substeps.instruction: Prepare a 10 % or 12 % polyacrylamide gel.
Load each fraction (suggest loading 1/1000 of the total volume for clear read‑out).
If samples are viscous (e.g., uninduced or induced cell suspensions), sonicate briefly in a bath sonicator to reduce viscosity before loading.
Stain the gel with Coomassie Brilliant Blue and document band patterns.

steps.title: Combine pure VDAC1 fractions
steps.instruction: Pool the fractions that show a single, strong VDAC1 band based on the SDS‑PAGE results.

steps.title: Concentrate protein to 300 µM
steps.instruction: Use a 10 kDa MWCO centrifugal filter to concentrate pooled VDAC1 to ~300 µM (~10 mg mL⁻¹).

substeps.instruction: Place the pooled protein in a 15 mL 10 kDa Amicon Ultra filter housed in a 50 mL plastic conical tube.
Centrifuge at 4 000 × g for 5 min at 20 °C–24 °C.
Pipette the retentate up and down or gently shake the filter to prevent protein sticking to the membrane.
Repeat centrifugation and mixing steps until the desired final volume (≈1 mL) and concentration are reached.

steps.title: Aliquot and store concentrated protein
steps.instruction: Dispense the concentrated VDAC1 into 1 mL aliquots and store at –20 °C.

substeps.instruction: Aliquot ~1 mL (≈10 mg protein) per tube; no glycerol or flash‑freezing is required because the protein is denatured.
Seal tubes and store at –20 °C (denatured VDAC1 remains stable for several months).

steps.title: Normalize fluorescence data
steps.instruction: Convert raw fluorescence traces to relative values by dividing by the initial fluorescence average.

substeps.instruction: Open the data file in Excel (or comparable spreadsheet software).
Calculate the average fluorescence of the first 50 s of the recording.
Divide every data point by this average to obtain normalized fluorescence.

steps.title: Fit data to two‑phase decay
steps.instruction: Apply a double‑exponential model to the normalized fluorescence data to extract kinetic parameters.

substeps.instruction: Import the normalized dataset into GraphPad Prism.
Plot normalized fluorescence versus time.
Select Prism’s built‑in two‑phase decay (double exponential) non‑linear regression model.
Fit the data and record the two rate constants and the plateau (endpoint) value.

steps.title: Quantify and perform statistical analysis
steps.instruction: Analyze processed data according to the methods described by Jahn et al.

substeps.instruction: Refer to Jahn et al. (reference 3) for detailed data‑processing steps and to the provided source files for sample datasets.

description: The voltage-dependent anion channel (VDAC) is the most abundant protein in the outer mitochondrial membrane and plays many roles in mitochondrial physiology, ranging from ion and metabolite permeation to apoptosis and phospholipid scrambling. To study its many functions in vitro, purified protein is needed. Overexpression of VDAC in eukaryotic cells is challenging as it results in poor yields, and purification from tissue does not allow separation of the different isoforms. Herein, we describe a bacterial expression protocol to obtain high yields of pure and functional VDAC1, suitable for functional and structural studies. This protocol typically increases yield by 1.5- to 2-fold over protocols that rely entirely on dialysis during refolding, with some batch-to-batch variation of about 10%–20%. We detail the production of 6xHis-tagged VDAC1. Mouse and human VDAC1 (mVDAC1 and hVDAC1, respectively) are essentially identical proteins, differing in only 4 amino acids, and their structure is almost identical. Consequently, the protocol we describe can be used to produce and purify both proteins and is also readily applicable to point mutants of these proteins. We express VDAC1 in E. coli where it forms cytoplasmic aggregates called inclusion bodies (Figure 1). The cells are lysed to release the aggregates, which are then denatured and solubilized in urea, before being subjected to Ni-NTA affinity chromatography to purify the protein (Figure 2). Purified VDAC1 is refolded by removing urea and adding detergent. Size exclusion chromatography is used as a final polishing step to eliminate residual urea and any aggregated or multimerized protein (Figure 4). 1 L of bacterial cell culture typically yields 5 mg of refolded monomeric VDAC1. We describe procedures to assess VDAC1 channel and phospholipid scramblase activity via fluorescence-based assays (Figure 7). Channel activity does not depend on the quaternary structure of VDAC1, but scramblase activity requires VDAC1 dimers.
